title: A Deal to Stop the Bombs — But Will It Last?
summary: Imagine a war so big it shakes the whole world — making food and gas prices jump, and hurting millions of families. That’s been happening in the Middle East for over three months. But this week, something surprising happened: U.S. President Trump and Iran’s President Pezeshkian signed a paper called a memorandum of understanding. It’s a promise to stop all fighting and talk about peace. Trump even posted, “Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!” because a key waterway, the Strait of Hormuz, will reopen. But here’s the catch: the deal only gives them 60 days to work things out. And right away, problems popped up. Israel, which wasn’t part of the talks, kept bombing Lebanon, where it’s fighting a group called Hezbollah. Israeli leaders say the deal doesn’t protect them, so they won’t stop. Iran says Israel must leave southern Lebanon, or the war isn’t really over. Vice President Vance warned that Trump is Israel’s best friend right now. So, is this a real step toward peace, or just a pause before more trouble? The whole world is watching.
why_it_matters: This deal could lower gas prices and make it cheaper for your family to fill the car or buy food from faraway places.

A powerful armed group based in Lebanon that often fights against Israel.

background_read: The Middle East is a region that includes countries like Iran, Israel, and Lebanon, where there have been many conflicts over land and religion.
The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow water passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the ocean) is so important because about one-fifth of the world's oil travels through it.
Hezbollah (a Lebanese armed group supported by Iran) has fought against Israel many times, which is part of the larger tensions.
Article_Structure: WHO: U.S. President Trump and Iran's President Pezeshkian, with Vice President Vance and Israel.
WHAT: They signed a memorandum of understanding to stop all fighting for 60 days, but Israel kept bombing Lebanon.
WHERE: The Middle East, especially the Strait of Hormuz and southern Lebanon.
WHY: The war had been causing food and gas prices to rise worldwide, so the deal aims to bring peace and reopen the oil route.

perspectives.description: They hope the deal will stop the fighting and help families in the Middle East live safely again. It could also make oil and food cheaper worldwide.
They say the deal leaves them in danger because Hezbollah is still attacking, and they don't trust Iran to keep its promises.
Many countries are watching to see if the deal will actually work, because past agreements in the region have often failed.
